tier_reason: Every number in the record matches the README tables (girl.bmp, 1034.db, enwik9bwt on i7-6700, gcc 8.3, 2019-08), which are first-party TurboBench runs; the benchmark harness (powturbo/TurboBench) is public but the README states no flags and the 2019 build flags are unknown (only the HEAD TurboBench makefile shows -O3 -march=haswell for TurboRLE), so it falls short of A and stays C.

corrections.baseline: rle8 (rainerzufalldererste/rle8 as of 2019, an SSE/AVX2 8-bit run length encoder, one configuration 'rle8 1'; that repository has since become hypersonic-rle-kit) and Mespotine RLE (MRLE); memcpy shown as a reference row. None of the general-lossless category baselines (zlib, zstd, lz4, brotli, xz) appear in the README tables.
corrections.hardware: Intel Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz (x86 tables for girl.bmp, 1034.db and enwik9bwt); ARM A73 ODROID-N2 1.8GHz (second set of tables covering only girl.bmp and enwik9bwt, with no rle8 row since rle8 is x86 SSE/AVX2 only)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc 8.3 (tables dated 2019-08); flags not stated in the README. The current TurboBench makefile builds the TurboRLE objects with -O3 -march=haswell -w -fstrict-aliasing -falign-loops=32 -DNDEBUG on x86_64, but that is the HEAD makefile, not the 2019 revision. The in-repo ./trle test tool (trle.c) benchmarks trle, srle and mrle but not rle8, so the rle8 rows can only come from TurboBench.
corrections.caveats: Tier C: first-party tables dated 2019-08 with compiler and CPU stated but no flags in the README; TurboBench is public but its 2019 build flags are not documented, and TurboRLE's own code has changed since (decoder commits as recent as 2026-07). The baselines are other RLE libraries, not the general-lossless category incumbents (zlib, zstd, lz4, brotli, xz). The 'up to 12x / 6x' claims cherry-pick the best variant per file (srle 8 vs rle8 on girl.bmp compression; srle 8 vs rle8 on enwik9bwt decompression); trle decompresses girl.bmp slower than rle8 and mrle (11385 vs 11998 and 12302 MB/s). The rle8 baseline is stale: its successor, hypersonic-rle-kit (same repository, BSD-2-Clause), benchmarks TurboRLE commit 7f6e486 (April 2023, AVX2 enabled) on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X with Visual Studio 2022, and its own 8-bit codecs decode several times faster than trle and srle 8 at similar ratios (enwik9.bwt: '8 Bit 3LUT Short' 40.34% ratio, 765.3 MiB/s encode, 3,046.5 MiB/s decode vs trle 42.0%, 697.6 and 2,062.9 MiB/s; '8 Bit' decodes at 16,097.6 MiB/s vs srle 8 6,095.1 MiB/s); trle keeps the best plain-RLE ratio on 1034.db (17.4% vs 18.55%). That contradicts the README's 'No other RLE compress or decompress faster with better compression'. The memcpy row and the 'faster than memcpy' claim apply only to srle 64 compression of highly compressible data (girl.bmp: 16269 vs 13978 MB/s, output 4.9% of input). GPL-2.0-or-later (copyleft).

notes: Numbers verified exactly against the README; tier C stands. Main shortcomings: off-baseline (RLE libraries only, no zlib/zstd/lz4 rows), cherry-picked 'up to' ratios, and a stale 2019 rle8 baseline that its own successor hypersonic-rle-kit now beats in third-party (competitor-run) 2023 tables. The repository now lives at github.com/powturbo/Turbo-Run-Length-Encoding (TurboRLE redirects there); hypersonic-rle-kit (rainerzufalldererste/rle8) is not in the catalog and is a lead.

tier_reason: ranking_1.html in ga-developers/ga-benchmark-runs (2020.02.05) shows exactly the recorded medal counts from the independent community suite ga-developers/ga-benchmark (Google Benchmark, random arguments, DoNotOptimize, 30 repetitions); GCC 7.4.0 Release is stated but no CPU model and no explicit flags beyond CMake Release, so not A; a peer-reviewed gafro paper (IEEE RAM 2024, snippet only) also reports GATL and Versor as the fastest GA libraries, supporting B.

corrections.caveats: Tier B: independent community suite (ga-developers/ga-benchmark, GPL-3.0, code public, run published in ga-benchmark-runs) but the context line gives no CPU model (8 x 1992 MHz, WSL1 kernel 4.4.0-18362-Microsoft) and no flags beyond CMake Release with GCC 7.4.0, and the run is from February 2020, so the Versor revision tested may differ from current devel. The result is a medal ranking against other geometric algebra libraries, not a speedup against the geometry-spatial category incumbents (Boost.Geometry, CGAL, GEOS) or any standard-library facility, and gives no time ratios. Medals are positions by exact equality of mean CPU time (gabm.py make_ranking), and 1,043 golds were awarded over 323 cases (derived from page data), so GATL, Versor, Gaalop and Gaalet share first place in most cases: a Versor gold means tied-fastest, not uniquely fastest, and its 246 golds vs GATL's 247 is a tie. Gaalop and Gaalet counts are depressed by 59 compilation-error faults each. The inverse-kinematics algorithm is excluded from the medal table (IGNORED_GROUPS). The gafro paper (Loew and Calinon, IEEE Robotics and Automation Magazine 2024, arXiv 2310.19090) forked ga-benchmark and states that GATL and Versor were previously reported to be the fastest GA libraries (read from search snippets only; arXiv and idiap.ch are blocked). The suite's install script clones github.com/wolftype/versor; the Versor README itself has no numbers (prose 'fast' and 'on steroids' only).

notes: Medal table numbers match the page exactly; tier B confirmed. Main shortcomings: off-category baseline (other GA libraries, not Boost.Geometry/CGAL/GEOS), ranking without speed ratios where golds are mostly shared ties with GATL/Gaalop/Gaalet, no CPU model, 2020-era run on WSL1. Metadata checked: BSD-2-Clause, 327 stars, 54 forks, last commit 2025-11-03 on devel.

tier_reason: All 15 single-thread width-4 logs in data/Euro-Par-2016-conference/hsw_benchmark.gnu-5.3.0_Vc-1.2.0_conditional reproduce the recorded means and ratios; benchmark code is public (flwende/simd_benchmarks src/<kernel>/kernel_reference.cpp and kernel_simd_class_vectorization.cpp, src/common/benchmark.cpp), compiler GNU 5.3.0 and flags (makefile.gnu, unchanged since the 2016-08-16 commit that added the data) and CPU (Xeon E5-2680v3 @ 1.9 GHz, notes.txt) are stated, run by third parties for a peer-reviewed Euro-Par 2016 paper.

corrections.baseline: Sequential reference loop that calls an out-of-line scalar kernel per element (kernel_reference.cpp is compiled as a separate translation unit without LTO, so the loop cannot be auto-vectorized) using std::exp, std::log and std::sqrt from <cmath> (GCC 5.3.0 libstdc++ forwarding to glibc libm), built with -O3 -ftree-vectorize -ffast-math -mavx2 -mfma
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GNU 5.3.0, Vc 1.2.0; makefile.gnu in flwende/simd_benchmarks: g++ -O3 -fopenmp -std=c++11 -ftree-vectorize -ffast-math -fopt-info-vec-optimized -mavx2 -mfma -D__AVX2__ -DBENCHMARK_FUNC_<F>_<F> -DSIMD_WIDTH_LOGICAL_REAL64=4 -DDEBUG, plus -DCONDITIONAL_CALL for all executables (notes.txt); Vc linked from $(VC_ROOT)/lib/libVc.a. The makefile and the data come from the same August 2016 commits (notes dated 2016-08-15, last commit 2016-08-16).
corrections.claimed_speedup: Third-party data (mean time per loop iteration, GCC 5.3.0, Haswell, 1 thread, SIMD width 4), Vc (simd_class_vectorization) vs sequential std:: reference, ratios derived from page data: simple EXP 7.8586e-09 s vs 2.477e-08 s (3.15x), simple LOG 8.14221e-09 vs 3.58324e-08 (4.40x), simple SQRT 6.41381e-09 vs 1.14677e-08 (1.79x); conditional_math_call EXP 2.27x, LOG 2.39x, SQRT 5.07x (3.3077e-09 vs 1.67538e-08); early_return EXP 2.87x, LOG 3.16x, SQRT 4.30x; nested_branching EXP 1.56x, LOG 1.64x, SQRT 2.19x; while_loop EXP 1.34x, LOG 1.62x, SQRT 0.78x (Vc slower: 5.97054e-08 vs 4.6563e-08). In the same logs plain OpenMP 4.x 'omp declare simd' (explicit_vectorization) reaches only 1.00-1.09x and is slower than Vc in all 15 cases, the paper's enhanced OpenMP version beats Vc in 8 of 15 cases, and hand-written AVX2 intrinsics (manual_vectorization) beat Vc in 12 of 15 cases (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: Vc's own README and docs carry no benchmark numbers; the evidence is third-party data from the Euro-Par 2016 paper 'Portable SIMD Performance with OpenMP 4.x Compiler Directives' (Wende et al.), whose subject is OpenMP, not Vc. The baseline is a deliberately scalar loop: the reference kernel sits in a separate translation unit and is called once per element with std::exp/std::log/std::sqrt, so the gains measure 4-wide SIMD with Vc's vector math (and one call per 4 elements) against scalar libm with one call per element, not against an auto-vectorized loop. Vc is slower than the reference on while_loop SQRT (0.78x) and hand-written intrinsics beat Vc in 12 of 15 single-thread cases. Only single-thread width-4 GNU logs were read (threads12, SIMD width 8, Intel 16.0.3, Clang 3.9.0(pre), KNC and KNL logs not read). Arrays are small (n = 8192 doubles, cache-resident) and the -DCONDITIONAL_CALL build adds a per-element mask to every kernel. The HEAD build.gnu sets VC_AVAILABLE=no, so reproducing the Vc rows needs VC_AVAILABLE=yes and VC_ROOT set. The data is from Vc 1.2.0 (2016); Vc is now 1.4.x and its README says it is in maintenance mode and no longer actively developed (pull requests with bug fixes are still reviewed), recommending std::simd (experimental in GCC 11 libstdc++) instead. The Vc authors' own paper and Kretz's dissertation were unreachable (host blocked), so no first-party numbers were checked. The data repo has only 9 commits and 6 stars.

notes: All 15 ratios re-derived from the logs and match; tier A confirmed (public code, GCC 5.3.0, makefile flags from the same 2016 commit, Xeon E5-2680v3). Corrections: the baseline is a scalar out-of-line loop over std::exp/log/sqrt (<cmath>, libstdc++), so baseline_in_list and compared_against_cpp_std_directly become true; plain omp simd is slower than Vc, manual intrinsics faster in 12 of 15. Shortcomings: SIMD-vs-scalar comparison by construction, 0.78x on while_loop SQRT, 2016 Vc 1.2.0 data, project in maintenance mode (std::simd is the successor).
